newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegro bourse reports first share sale.
newsitem.headline: Montenegro bourse reports first share sale.

text.p: The Montenegro Stock Exchange witnessed the first sale of shares last week and bourse officials said on Monday it was an encouraging sign for the fledgling financial market of the small Yugoslav republic.
Podgorica-based Hipotekarna banka last Thursday offered for sale 104 shares. The stock, first issued in 1993 and 1994, was bought back from original holders and placed on the bourse.
Hipotekarna sold the entire lot of 104 shares substantially above their face value of 5,123 dinars, bourse chief Milasin Borovic told Reuters.
Of the total, 54 shares were sold at 5,500 dinars each while the remainder fetched 5,400 dinars per share, Borovic said.
According to the bourse report, shares were bought by five Montenegrin companies and one firm from Belgrade.
Vanja Perovic, in charge of the share trading, said this was the first time the bourse was established in 1993 that secondary trading had appeared in some form.
In its three-year history, the Podgorica-based stock exchange jas dealt only with short-term securities and giro-money, lacking any long-term instrument.

The first ever placement of shares was recorded in February 1995, when Agroosiguranje insurer listed its stock. "But that was only the placement and no real bourse trading has ever happened," Perovic said.
Despite a large number of shareholding companies in Montenegro, none of them have dared offer their stock on the market, fearing the market price would be far below the face value.
But Borovic said companies should be encouraged by the Hipotekarna experience.

"This sale proved the market price could easily go above the par if stock is sold by a bank or a company with good commercial and managerial record," Borovic said, adding that Hipotekarna was a solid commercial bank, regularly paying dividend to its shareholders.
New stock-owners will be able to sell shares if they want funds back. But it was premature to expect genuine secondary trading to develop, Perovic said.

"It is still too early under present circumstances to expect new shareholders to sell in order to make capital gains. Such activity may develop during 1997 when we hope to see more listings on the bourse," Perovic said.

"This is only the very beginning. Montenegro has created a good economic and investment climate because it successfully rounded up the first stage of privatisation. We expect to see more shares quoted and sold on the Montenegro bourse in the future," Borovic said.
